examTakeaway: A new unilateral pleural effusion with fever is sampled by thoracentesis before antibiotics are chosen from guesswork.
scenario: A 63-year-old man has fever of 38.5 C, a cough, and shortness of breath. The film shows a right effusion occupying about one third of the hemithorax. Blood pressure is 130/70 mm Hg. He has no heart-failure history. The fluid has not been sampled.
question: Which plan is the most appropriate next step?
options: A chest tube with no fluid analysis
explanation: A new unilateral pleural effusion with fever is sampled by thoracentesis before antibiotics are chosen from guesswork. Thoracentesis is the IDSA step that classifies a parapneumonic effusion. Diuretics for three days first fit bilateral failure, which this one-sided febrile effusion is not. A chest tube with no fluid analysis drains before you know the fluid is complicated. Antibiotics with no tap miss an empyema. CT surgery before any sample skips the fluid diagnosis.

examTakeaway: Sepsis with hypotension and a lactate of 4 is treated at once with intravenous crystalloid and antibiotics, not with a pressor before any fluid.
scenario: A 72-year-old woman with pneumonia has a blood pressure of 82/50 mm Hg and a lactate of 4.6 mmol/L. She has received no fluid yet. She is confused. Cultures are being drawn. There is no sign of fluid overload.
question: Which plan is the most appropriate next step?
options: A steroid as the first drug
Crystalloid at 30 mL/kg and an antibiotic now
Wait for the culture to choose an antibiotic
correctAnswer: Crystalloid at 30 mL/kg and an antibiotic now
explanation: Sepsis with hypotension and a lactate of 4 is treated at once with intravenous crystalloid and antibiotics, not with a pressor before any fluid. Crystalloid at 30 mL/kg and an antibiotic now follows the 2021 sepsis hour-1 bundle in a patient who is not volume overloaded. Norepinephrine before any fluid skips the fluid she has not received. Wait for the culture to choose an antibiotic delays the dose. A steroid as the first drug is not the opening move. Colloid as the required fluid is not preferred over crystalloid.

examTakeaway: A high-risk Ixodes tick that was attached for at least 36 hours is treated with one dose of doxycycline, not with a three-week course.
scenario: A 40-year-old man pulled off an engorged deer-tick after a weekend in an endemic county. The tick was attached for about 48 hours. He has no rash and feels well. He is not pregnant and takes no interacting drug. It has been a few hours since removal.
question: Which plan is the most appropriate next step?
options: Serology today and treatment only if positive
explanation: A high-risk Ixodes tick that was attached for at least 36 hours is treated with one dose of doxycycline, not with a three-week course. One 200 mg dose of doxycycline is the CDC prophylaxis when the tick is engorged, the area is endemic, and prophylaxis can start within 72 hours. Doxycycline for 21 days treats disease he does not have. Serology today and treatment only if positive is too early for antibodies. Amoxicillin for 14 days is not the prophylactic regimen. No prophylaxis ignores a high-risk bite.

examTakeaway: A dog bite to the hand is treated with amoxicillin-clavulanate, and the wound is not closed tightly.
scenario: A 24-year-old woman was bitten on the hand by a neighbor's dog six hours ago. The wound is a deep puncture. She is not allergic to penicillin. Her tetanus immunization is current. The dog is well and vaccinated.
question: Which plan is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: A dog bite to the hand is treated with amoxicillin-clavulanate, and the wound is not closed tightly. Amoxicillin-clavulanate and an open wound covers Pasteurella and follows IDSA care for a hand bite. Cephalexin alone misses Pasteurella. Tight suture closure seals a hand puncture. Metronidazole alone misses the aerobic bite organisms. No antibiotic is inadequate for this location.

examTakeaway: Exertional heat stroke is cooled with ice-water immersion, and acetaminophen does not lower this temperature.
scenario: A 19-year-old runner collapses at the end of a race. He is confused. Rectal temperature is 41.3 C. The skin is hot and dry. Blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. There is no tonic-clonic activity.
question: Which plan is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Exertional heat stroke is cooled with ice-water immersion, and acetaminophen does not lower this temperature. Ice-water immersion is the 2024 fastest cooling method for this rectal temperature and confusion. Acetaminophen acts on a hypothalamic set point he does not have. Dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia, not exertional heat stroke. Oral fluids only do not cool a confused runner. Antibiotics treat infection, not this collapse.

examTakeaway: An acetaminophen level above the treatment line is treated with N-acetylcysteine, without waiting for the aminotransferase to rise.
scenario: A 17-year-old girl swallowed a bottle of acetaminophen about eight hours ago. The serum level plots above the treatment line. AST and ALT are still normal. She is awake and has vomited once. She is not pregnant.
question: Which drug is the most appropriate next step?
options: Activated charcoal as the only treatment
explanation: An acetaminophen level above the treatment line is treated with N-acetylcysteine, without waiting for the aminotransferase to rise. N-acetylcysteine is indicated now by the 2020 treatment line, eight hours after the ingestion. Activated charcoal as the only treatment is too late to be the sole therapy. Wait until the ALT rises misses the window in which the antidote works best. Naloxone reverses opioids. Fomepizole treats toxic alcohols.

examTakeaway: Wernicke encephalopathy is treated with thiamine before glucose, because glucose alone can worsen the injury.
scenario: A 55-year-old man with daily heavy drinking is confused and ataxic. The eyes beat horizontally on lateral gaze. He has eaten almost nothing for days. A fingerstick glucose is 58 mg/dL and the team is about to infuse dextrose.
question: Which vitamin comes before the dextrose?
explanation: Wernicke encephalopathy is treated with thiamine before glucose, because glucose alone can worsen the injury. Thiamine is given before the dextrose in this confused, ataxic drinker with nystagmus. Folate does not treat Wernicke encephalopathy. Vitamin B12 treats a different cord syndrome. Vitamin C treats scurvy. No vitamin is needed leaves the mammillary injury exposed to a glucose load.

examTakeaway: Myxedema coma is treated with intravenous levothyroxine and a stress-dose steroid, without waiting for the TSH to return.
scenario: A 68-year-old woman is obtunded. Temperature is 34.4 C, heart rate is 46 bpm, and sodium is 124 mEq/L. She stopped levothyroxine months ago. The TSH has been sent and is not back. Blood pressure is 88/60 mm Hg. Blood glucose is 70 mg/dL.
question: Which plan is the most appropriate next step?
options: Warming blankets as the only treatment
explanation: Myxedema coma is treated with intravenous levothyroxine and a stress-dose steroid, without waiting for the TSH to return. Intravenous levothyroxine and hydrocortisone is the 2014 treatment, and the steroid covers coexisting adrenal failure. Wait for the TSH delays a life-threatening replacement. Oral levothyroxine only is poorly absorbed in this state and skips the steroid. Warming blankets as the only treatment do not replace hormone. Antibiotics and no thyroid hormone miss the cause.

examTakeaway: Adrenal crisis is treated with intravenous hydrocortisone and saline at once, and the cosyntropin test does not come first.
scenario: A 50-year-old man on prednisone 20 mg daily for years has been vomiting for two days and missed his doses. Blood pressure is 78/50 mm Hg. Sodium is 128 mEq/L and potassium is 5.7 mEq/L. He is confused. No cosyntropin result is available.
question: Which plan is the most appropriate next step?
options: Delay steroids until the cosyntropin result
explanation: Adrenal crisis is treated with intravenous hydrocortisone and saline at once, and the cosyntropin test does not come first. Intravenous hydrocortisone and saline now replaces glucocorticoid and volume in a hypotensive patient who stopped chronic prednisone. Delay steroids until the cosyntropin result waits through shock, and a dose of dexamethasone would be the only steroid that leaves the test interpretable if a test were still desired. Fludrocortisone tablets alone does not treat acute crisis and he cannot keep pills down. Insulin treats hyperglycemia and would worsen this picture. Antibiotics as the only drug miss cortisol.

examTakeaway: Symptomatic hypercalcemia is treated with intravenous saline first, and a loop diuretic is not the opening drug.
scenario: A 67-year-old woman with a new lung mass is confused. Calcium is 14.4 mg/dL and albumin is 4.0 g/dL. The ECG shows a short QT interval. Blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. She has not received fluid.
question: Which plan is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: Symptomatic hypercalcemia is treated with intravenous saline first, and a loop diuretic is not the opening drug. Intravenous normal saline restores the volume that calciuresis needs. Furosemide first worsens dehydration. A bisphosphonate before any fluid works too slowly to be the first act. Observation leaves a calcium of 14.4 mg/dL and confusion. Calcitonin as the only drug lowers calcium briefly and does not replace volume.

examTakeaway: Graves disease in the first trimester is treated with propylthiouracil, not with methimazole and not with radioiodine.
scenario: A 28-year-old woman at 8 weeks of pregnancy has tremor, a pulse of 120 bpm, and a diffuse goiter. TSH is suppressed and free T4 is twice normal. Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin is positive. She has no heart failure.
question: Which plan is the most appropriate next step?
options: A beta blocker as the only drug
explanation: Graves disease in the first trimester is treated with propylthiouracil, not with methimazole and not with radioiodine. Propylthiouracil is the 2017 choice before 16 weeks because methimazole has a higher risk of congenital malformations. Methimazole is avoided in this trimester. Radioiodine is contraindicated in pregnancy. Thyroidectomy this week is for a drug failure or a huge goiter, not the first step. A beta blocker as the only drug slows the pulse and leaves her thyrotoxic.

examTakeaway: Hyperemesis with poor intake is given thiamine before dextrose, so glucose does not precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy.
scenario: A 24-year-old woman at 10 weeks has vomited for a week and cannot keep water down. Urine ketones are large. She is dizzy. The team plans intravenous dextrose. She has not received vitamins. Fetal heart motion is present.
question: Which plan is the most appropriate next step?
options: Oral sips as the only treatment
explanation: Hyperemesis with poor intake is given thiamine before dextrose, so glucose does not precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy. Thiamine, then intravenous dextrose follows ACOG care for prolonged vomiting before a glucose infusion. Dextrose before any thiamine risks that injury. Immediate termination is not the treatment of hyperemesis when the fetus is viable and she has not yet received fluids and antiemetics. Oral sips as the only treatment have already failed. Antibiotics treat an infection she does not have.

examTakeaway: A positive group B streptococcus culture is treated with penicillin during labor, not by cesarean delivery for that result alone.
scenario: A 32-year-old woman at 38 weeks is in labor. A rectovaginal culture at 36 weeks grew group B streptococcus. She has no penicillin allergy. Membranes ruptured two hours ago. The tracing is reassuring and labor is progressing.
question: Which plan is the most appropriate next step?
options: Antibiotics after the cord is clamped
Treat her partner and give her nothing
explanation: A positive group B streptococcus culture is treated with penicillin during labor, not by cesarean delivery for that result alone. Intravenous penicillin during labor is the CDC regimen when she has no allergy. Cesarean delivery for the culture does not replace intrapartum antibiotics and is not indicated by a reassuring tracing. Antibiotics after the cord is clamped miss the window that protects the newborn. Treat her partner and give her nothing does not prevent early-onset disease. Clindamycin despite no allergy is for a high-risk penicillin allergy.

examTakeaway: A boggy uterus and postpartum bleeding are treated with uterine massage and oxytocin, not with hysterectomy as the first move.
scenario: A 29-year-old woman has just delivered the placenta. She is bleeding briskly and the uterus is soft. Estimated loss is 900 mL. There is no cervical laceration. Blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. She has no hypertension.
question: Which plan is the most appropriate next step?
options: Uterine artery embolization as the first step
explanation: A boggy uterus and postpartum bleeding are treated with uterine massage and oxytocin, not with hysterectomy as the first move. Massage and oxytocin is the ACOG first step for atony. Hysterectomy is a last resort after drugs and procedures fail. Uterine artery embolization as the first step skips the uterotonic. Observation lets the bleeding continue. Antibiotics as the only treatment address infection, not a soft uterus.

examTakeaway: An unsensitized Rh-negative woman receives anti-D immunoglobulin at 28 weeks.
scenario: A 27-year-old woman is Rh-negative. At 28 weeks the antibody screen is negative. The father of the baby is Rh-positive. She has had no bleeding and no procedure. She feels fetal movement.
question: Which plan is the most appropriate next step?
options: No anti-D because the screen is negative
explanation: An unsensitized Rh-negative woman receives anti-D immunoglobulin at 28 weeks. Anti-D immunoglobulin now is the ACOG dose when the antibody screen is still negative. No anti-D because the screen is negative confuses unsensitized status with a reason to skip prophylaxis. Anti-D only after delivery misses the routine antepartum dose. Amniocentesis to decide is not required. Anti-D for her partner does not protect her pregnancy.

examTakeaway: Number needed to treat is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction.
scenario: A 22-year-old student reads a trial. Death occurs in 10 of 100 people on placebo and in 5 of 100 people on the new drug. No one left the study. She is asked for the number needed to treat.
question: Which number is the NNT?
explanation: Number needed to treat is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction. 20 is 1 divided by the absolute reduction from 0.10 to 0.05. 5 is the number of deaths on the drug, not the number needed to treat. 10 is the number of deaths on placebo. 2 is the relative risk of 0.5 inverted loosely and is not the number needed to treat. 50 would require an absolute reduction of 0.02.

examTakeaway: Intention-to-treat analysis keeps every randomized person in the assigned group, including those who stopped the drug.
scenario: A 22-year-old student reviews a randomized trial. Twenty people assigned to the drug stopped it because of nausea. The investigators still count those twenty in the drug group. A classmate wants them removed.
question: Which analysis keeps those twenty in the drug group?
explanation: Intention-to-treat analysis keeps every randomized person in the assigned group, including those who stopped the drug. Intention to treat is the analysis the investigators used. Per protocol drops people who did not complete the assigned drug. As treated moves them into whatever they actually took. Case series has no randomized groups. Crossover gives each person both treatments in sequence, which this design did not.

examTakeaway: Lead-time bias makes screening look helpful because the clock starts earlier, while the date of death is unchanged.
scenario: A 22-year-old student compares two groups who die of the same cancer at the same age. The screened group learned of the cancer three years earlier, so survival after diagnosis looks longer. The unscreened group was diagnosed later.
question: Which bias produced the longer survival after diagnosis?
options: Selection of a healthier screened group
explanation: Lead-time bias makes screening look helpful because the clock starts earlier, while the date of death is unchanged. Lead-time bias is the earlier clock in this comparison. Length-time bias enriches a screened sample with slow-growing tumors. Recall bias affects how people remember exposures. Selection of a healthier screened group would change the age at death, which is the same here. Confounding by smoking is not described.

examTakeaway: A hazard ratio of 0.6 whose 95 percent interval excludes 1 is a reduction, not a null result.
scenario: A 22-year-old student reads a trial of a drug to prevent stroke. The hazard ratio is 0.60 and the 95 percent confidence interval is 0.40 to 0.85. She must say what that interval allows.
question: Which conclusion fits the interval?
options: The result is null because the ratio is under 1
The interval proves the drug helps every patient
The p value must be above 0.05
The drug was associated with a lower hazard
correctAnswer: The drug was associated with a lower hazard
explanation: A hazard ratio of 0.6 whose 95 percent interval excludes 1 is a reduction, not a null result. The drug was associated with a lower hazard because the entire interval is below 1. The drug raised the hazard would require a ratio above 1. The result is null because the ratio is under 1 misreads a ratio below 1 as no effect. The interval proves the drug helps every patient overclaims what a hazard ratio can say. The p value must be above 0.05 is the opposite of an interval that excludes 1.

examTakeaway: Whole cow milk before the first birthday causes iron deficiency and is stopped, with iron replaced.
scenario: An 11-month-old boy has been drinking whole cow milk instead of formula for two months and eats few solids. Hemoglobin is 8.2 g/dL, MCV is 66 fL, and ferritin is 6 ng/mL. He is otherwise playful. Stool is guaiac negative.
question: Which feeding plan is required?
options: Stop cow milk and give iron
Continue cow milk and add juice
correctAnswer: Stop cow milk and give iron
explanation: Whole cow milk before the first birthday causes iron deficiency and is stopped, with iron replaced. Stop cow milk and give iron removes the milk that irritates the gut and crowds out iron-rich food, and it replaces the missing iron. Continue cow milk and add juice keeps the cause. Vitamin B12 injections treat a macrocytic anemia. Bone marrow biopsy is not needed when the ferritin is 6 ng/mL and the diet explains it. A proton-pump inhibitor does not replace iron.

examTakeaway: An exclusively breastfed infant needs 400 IU of vitamin D daily, starting in the first days of life.
scenario: A 2-month-old girl is exclusively breastfed and growing along her curve. Her mother takes a prenatal vitamin. The infant takes no drops. The exam is normal and she has no rickets yet.
question: Which supplement does the infant need?
explanation: An exclusively breastfed infant needs 400 IU of vitamin D daily, starting in the first days of life. Vitamin D 400 IU daily is the 2008 recommendation even when the mother takes a prenatal vitamin and the exam is still normal. Whole cow milk is not used at two months. Fluoride drops are not started at this age when the water supply is the usual source later. Iron as the only supplement misses vitamin D; iron is considered around four months, not instead of vitamin D now. No supplement leaves her short of vitamin D.

examTakeaway: No words and no pointing at 18 months requires a hearing test and a developmental referral, not a wait until preschool.
scenario: An 18-month-old boy says no words and does not point or wave. He does not turn when his name is called. Pregnancy and birth were uncomplicated. He has never had a hearing test. His parents hope he will catch up by kindergarten.
question: Which plan is the most appropriate next step?
options: Diagnose autism today without any testing
A brain MRI as the first test
Hearing test and developmental referral now
correctAnswer: Hearing test and developmental referral now
explanation: No words and no pointing at 18 months requires a hearing test and a developmental referral, not a wait until preschool. Hearing test and developmental referral now matches the 2020 response to absent words, absent gestures, and no response to his name. Reassurance until age 4 misses the window for services. Antibiotics for otitis treat an infection he does not have. Diagnose autism today without any testing skips the hearing test that can mimic this picture. A brain MRI as the first test is not the opening evaluation.
